scenes.narration: In 2007, Nokia sold roughly half of all the smartphones on Earth.
scenes.subtitle: How an empire fell

scenes.narration: Its phones were in pockets from Helsinki to Jakarta. For a decade, it seemed untouchable.
scenes.query: busy city street crowd people walking

scenes.narration: It all began in Finland, a small country of about five and a half million people.
Founded in 1865 as a paper mill, the company reinvented itself again and again, from rubber boots to cables to electronics.
scenes.prompt: 19th century Finnish paper mill beside a river in winter, wooden buildings, smoke rising, dramatic light

scenes.narration: By the late nineties, Nokia had become the largest mobile phone maker in the world.
At its peak, roughly half of all smartphones sold carried the Nokia name.
Then, in 2007, Apple launched the iPhone.
scenes.query: hand using smartphone touchscreen close up

scenes.narration: Nokia's phones were still selling, but its software could not keep up.
scenes.prompt: an old generic candybar mobile phone with a green screen on a dark table, moody low key light, shallow depth of field

scenes.narration: In 2011, its new chief executive wrote to his staff: we have fallen behind, we have missed big trends, and we have lost time.
scenes.quote: We have fallen behind, we have missed big trends, and we have lost time.
scenes.author: Stephen Elop, 2011

scenes.narration: In 2013, Microsoft bought Nokia's phone business for about five and a half billion euros.
This is the story of how an empire lost its way.
